28afe46518:
This chapter re-examines the ordinary engineering disciplines: REST, JSON, async I/O, version control, the delivery life cycle, code review and refactoring. The twist is that one dependency in the system is a slow, metered, rate-limited and probabilistic model.

You know the basics from years of Spring services. So the chapter spends its time on what changes:

  • idempotency, when the expensive call is not the dangerous one;
  • validation, when output is well-formed but wrong;
  • concurrency, when the bottleneck is someone else's token bucket;
  • tests, when the function under test has no single right answer;
  • review, when the author of the diff is a model.
04fda7c288: Reading time: 2 to 2.5 hours  ·  Companion code, 18 runnable examples: ccdvf-companion/08-swe-foundations/ (run bash run_all.sh). Everything is offline, and the FastAPI examples use TestClient.
ba8d2577d7:
Neighbouring chapters: chapter 05 owns the Messages API error statuses and retry rules. Chapter 07 owns the Batch API. Chapter 10 owns prompt and model versioning, CLAUDE.md and settings.json. Chapter 12 covers debugging and trace analysis, chapter 14 HTTP, SSE and the SDK transport layer, and chapter 18 output handling.

This chapter owns the engineering practice around the call: the API you put in front of Claude, the contracts on its output, the concurrency model, the delivery pipeline, the tests and the reviews.
20e391c8b9:
The chapter rests on two sentences.

An LLM call is a remote dependency with four unusual properties: it takes seconds, it costs money per call, it is rate-limited by tokens rather than requests, and its output is untrusted even when it is well-formed, so every ordinary engineering practice still applies but each one moves its weight to a different place.

Make side effects idempotent rather than the model call, validate output in two layers (shape, then meaning), bound concurrency below someone else's quota, keep prompts in the same repository and pipeline as the code with an evaluation gate beside the unit tests, and put the model behind a narrow interface so the rest of the system can be tested with fakes and reviewed like any other code.
d5d4b61856:
Objective 2.4 lists "REST, JSON, async, version control, SDLC, code review, refactoring". At 7.4% it is the largest single sub-objective in Domain 2, larger than API mechanics (6.8%).

That tells you something about the exam's view of the job. Most of a Claude application is not Claude. It is an HTTP service, a set of JSON contracts, a concurrency model, a repository, a pipeline and a review culture.

The questions are judgment questions:

  • Which status code means a retry can help?
  • Why does a schema-valid answer still need checking?
  • Why is a synchronous client inside an async def handler a production incident?
  • Where does a prompt live, and what has to pass before a change to it ships?
  • What should a reviewer look for in a diff Claude wrote?
f295eed962:
If you have run Spring services for years, the danger is not ignorance. It is transfer. Most of your instincts are right, and a few are wrong in a way that matters.

  • The thread-per-request model that served you well for 20-millisecond database calls wastes threads on 20-second model calls.
  • A @Retryable on the service method that both asks the model and issues the refund will one day issue two refunds.
  • A contract test that asserts an exact response body cannot be written for a model.

Each section below states the familiar principle briefly. Then it spends its length on the place where the LLM case differs.
af0d4bc425: None of the practices in this chapter were invented for language models. Knowing where each one came from tells you what problem it solves. And that tells you what it does, and does not, protect you from when the dependency is a model.
15f36065bf:
Roy Fielding's 2000 dissertation described REST as the architectural style of the web: resources named by URLs, a uniform interface of methods, stateless requests, cacheable responses.

The HTTP specification (now RFC 9110) defines which methods are safe and which are idempotent. Safe means no intended side effects: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS. Idempotent means repeating the request has the same effect as sending it once: the safe methods plus PUT and DELETE. POST is neither.

The definition matters because networks fail in the middle. A client that sent a request and got no answer cannot know whether the server acted. If the method is idempotent, it can simply send it again. If not, it needs another mechanism.
d77f17d157:
That mechanism became widespread with payment APIs in the 2010s. Stripe popularised the Idempotency-Key request header. The client generates a unique key per logical operation, and the server stores the outcome under that key. A repeated POST with the same key returns the stored outcome instead of charging the card again.

An IETF draft (draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header) standardises the header. Check its current status before you cite it as a standard.

Telecom order systems have used the same pattern for decades under other names: a correlation id that the provisioning platform deduplicates on.
f074635dc1:
Douglas Crockford described JSON in the early 2000s as a subset of JavaScript object literals. It is now RFC 8259. JSON won over XML for web APIs because it was smaller, and it mapped directly to the data structures of dynamic languages. What it lost was a built-in schema language.

JSON Schema grew to fill that gap through a series of drafts (draft 4, 6, 7, 2019-09, 2020-12). It is the format the Claude API uses for tool input_schema and structured outputs. Note that the API accepts a subset of JSON Schema for strict structured outputs. Which keywords are supported is a detail to check in the docs, not to assume.
efede48933:
In 1999 Dan Kegel's "C10k problem" asked how one server could hold ten thousand concurrent connections, when each OS thread cost memory and context switches. The answer was event-driven I/O: one thread, many sockets, callbacks when data arrives (nginx, Node.js).

Python adopted the model in asyncio (Python 3.4, 2014) and the async/await syntax (3.5). Java took a different path. First came CompletableFuture (Java 8), then reactive libraries (Reactor, WebFlux), and finally virtual threads (Project Loom, final in Java 21, 2023). Virtual threads make blocking calls cheap again by parking a lightweight thread instead of an OS thread.

Both lines solve the same problem, and LLM calls are its extreme case. Each call holds a connection open for seconds while doing nothing.
25ba77ec60:
Michael Fagan formalised code inspection at IBM in 1976. The lightweight pull-request review most teams practise today arrived with distributed version control (git, 2005) and hosted forges. Continuous integration and continuous delivery made the pipeline, not the person, the gate for releases. Trunk-based development (short-lived branches merged daily behind feature flags) became the common answer to the merge pain of long-lived branches.

For LLM features all of this carries over, with one addition: an evaluation suite as a pipeline stage. Unit tests cannot tell you whether a prompt change made answers worse.
102b90610e:
Martin Fowler's Refactoring (1999) defined refactoring as changing structure without changing behaviour, in small steps protected by tests. Michael Feathers' Working Effectively with Legacy Code (2004) added characterization tests. These pin current behaviour, so you can refactor code that has no tests. Gerard Meszaros named the test doubles (dummy, stub, spy, mock, fake) in xUnit Test Patterns (2007). Alistair Cockburn's hexagonal architecture (ports and adapters, 2005) put external systems behind interfaces owned by the domain.

The modern twist has two parts. An LLM SDK is exactly the kind of external system these ideas were built for. And an AI assistant can now write the refactoring for you, which raises the stakes on the tests that check it.
eacacf489f:
Distractors are often a familiar practice applied at the wrong point:

  • "make the model call idempotent" (it is already harmless; the side effect is not);
  • "retry all errors" (4xx will fail identically);
  • "raise the thread pool size" (the limit is the provider's token bucket);
  • "assert the exact response text in a unit test" (sampled output varies).

The correct answer usually keeps the classic practice, and moves it to the place the LLM changes.
5d53e08695: Before the individual practices, let's pin down what is different about an LLM call compared with the downstream services you already integrate. Each property below drives a design decision later in the chapter. Most exam stems describe a symptom of one of them.
338edf0cee: Latency is in seconds and varies widely. A short classification on Haiku 5.5 may return in under a second. A long answer with extended thinking on Opus 5.5 can take a minute. Time-to-first-token and total time are different numbers, and the total grows with output length. That moves you to async I/O, to streaming for interactive paths (chapter 06), and to the 202-and-poll pattern for long work (section 05).
49d1190d1c: Every call costs money, and retries cost again. A retry storm against your database wastes CPU. A retry storm against Claude is a bill, plus an exhausted quota that also starves your other features in the same organisation. So the retry policy is a cost decision as well as a reliability one. It also pushes non-urgent bulk work to the Batch API (chapter 07).
8341ec663e: Rate limits are measured in tokens as well as requests. The API limits requests per minute, and input and output tokens per minute, per model class (chapter 05). Two requests can differ in cost to your quota by a factor of a thousand. So concurrency limits have to be set from token budgets, and adaptive limits (section 08) beat fixed thread pools.
070526517a: Output is sampled and untrusted. The same input can produce different text, and well-formed output can be wrong. Unit tests can pin everything around the call, but the model's behaviour needs statistical evaluation. Any action taken on model output needs validation. And any output that reaches a SQL query, a shell or an HTML page is untrusted input in the security sense (chapter 19).
dcf1e1d45f: Behaviour lives partly outside the code. A system prompt edit, a tool description tweak or a model ID change alters behaviour as much as a code change, often more. Those artefacts have to be versioned, reviewed and gated like code. Chapter 10 owns the mechanics; section 09 here covers the branching and review workflow.
fb071af390:
Two REST APIs meet in every Claude application. Downstream is Anthropic's: POST /v1/messages and its siblings (batches, files, models, token counting). Upstream is yours: the endpoints your web app, mobile app or partner systems call, which in turn call Claude.

The exam mostly asks about the second, because that is where your design choices live. Chapter 05 covers the Messages API's own request and error shapes. Here the question is how to design the API you put in front of it.
2dfb04f0e7:
The first design decision is what your resources are. A common first draft exposes the model as a verb: POST /ai/ask with a free-form prompt. That leaks your prompt design to every caller and makes every client a prompt engineer. It also gives you nothing to cache, audit or version.

Model your domain instead. A billing-dispute assistant has disputes, each with explanations and recommendations. A ticket system has tickets/{id}/triage. The model is an implementation detail of how a triage is produced.

Then when the prompt changes, the resource contract does not. And when you replace a model call with a rule for the easy cases, no client notices.
bc1c9dcdac:
Resource thinking also forces the questions REST was built to answer. Is producing a triage a creation (POST, a new resource with its own id, auditable later)? Or is it a computation on an existing resource (a GET whose result you may cache)?

For anything that drives an action, prefer creation. Store the triage with the prompt version, model ID and request-id that produced it, and return its URL. That gives you an audit trail for free. It also makes "why did the system do that?" answerable months later.
0c126217f5:
Here is the point the exam returns to most often, and where Spring instincts mislead.

POST /v1/messages is not idempotent in the HTTP sense: each call is billed and may return different text. But for a pure generation, running it twice has no effect on the world beyond cost.

The call that is dangerous to repeat is the side effect your code performs because of the output: the refund, the SIM swap, the email to the customer, the ticket in the NOC queue. A timeout between your service and its caller tells nobody whether that side effect happened.
d1f2047fb9:
Consider the shape of most LLM-driven actions: receive request, call the model, act on the decision, respond. A client-side timeout can fire at any point.

Suppose it fires after the action but before the response. The caller retries the whole request. The model is called again, which is fine; it only costs tokens. Then the action runs again, which is not fine. Example 02_retry_side_effect.py reproduces it with a SIM-swap handler and shows the output:
640ef983fa:
The fix is not to prevent the second model call. It is to make the action idempotent, with a key derived from the business operation, not from the attempt.

simswap:ORD-55 is the same on every retry, so provisioning returns the original result. A random UUID generated inside the handler would differ on each retry and protect nothing. The key must come from the caller (an Idempotency-Key header) or from a stable business identifier (order id, case id, ticket id plus action).
655f15f6b7:
When your own API performs the side effect, it needs to honour a key itself. The algorithm has four cases, and example 01_idempotency_key_server.py implements all four in FastAPI:

  • On a new key, record it as in flight, perform the work, and store the response.
  • On a repeated key with the same request body, return the stored response.
  • On a repeated key with a different body, reject with 422. The client reused a key for a different operation, which is a bug you want to surface.
  • On a repeated key while the first attempt is still running, return 409, so the client backs off rather than racing.

The first-writer-wins step must be atomic. In production that is a unique constraint (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING) or a conditional write in Redis or DynamoDB, not a read-then-write.
96b913ce62:
In Spring the same logic usually sits in a HandlerInterceptor or a servlet filter, so every POST controller gets it. Put the store in the same database as the business write, so the key and the effect commit together.

If the key store and the effect live in different systems, you have a dual-write problem. The usual answer is the transactional outbox you may already use for Kafka events. Write the business row and the outbox row in one transaction, and publish from the outbox.
47bdb37d69: Don't assume it. The design in this section doesn't need it: the SDK retries the model call freely, and only your side effects are keyed. Whether the Messages API or Batch API honours any idempotency header is a detail to check in the docs. The exam answer for a duplicated side effect is always to key the side effect.
77eb9c5a9d:
Status codes are a contract about two things: whose fault the failure is, and whether trying again can help.

  • 4xx says the request is wrong, so sending the same bytes again fails the same way.
  • 5xx says the server failed, so a later retry may succeed.
  • 429 is the exception inside 4xx: the request was fine, but you sent too many.

Chapter 05 lists every status the Claude API returns, including its non-standard 529 overloaded_error, and the retry rules for each. The engineering question here is different. What does your API return to its callers when Claude, or Claude's output, fails?
37a76a2aa1:
The wrong answer is to pass Anthropic's status through.

  • If your API key is revoked, Claude returns 401. Pass a 401 to your mobile app and it concludes the user is not authenticated, so it logs them out.
  • If Claude returns 400 because your code built an invalid request, a 400 to your caller blames them for your bug.
  • If Claude returns 429, your caller should see "temporarily unavailable, try in N seconds", not a hint that they exceeded a limit.

Map upstream failures onto your own contract, deliberately. Example 03_status_mapping.py implements this table and asserts each row:
b94c149583:
For the body, use a standard error format rather than inventing one per endpoint. RFC 9457 (Problem Details for HTTP APIs, which obsoletes RFC 7807) defines type, title, status, detail and instance. It allows extension members such as retryable and requestId. Spring 6 supports it directly through ProblemDetail and ErrorResponseException.

Always include your own correlation id. Log it next to Claude's request-id response header, so a support ticket can be traced to the exact model call.
85e4d676c5:
Some LLM work takes longer than any sensible HTTP timeout: summarising a 300-page contract, running an agent that makes twenty tool calls, generating a report from a batch.

Holding the request open is fragile. Load balancers and API gateways cut idle connections (often around 60 seconds by default; check your infrastructure). Mobile clients lose connectivity. And a retry after a dropped connection starts the whole expensive job again.
c61041f855:
The REST answer is asynchronous request-reply. POST /summaries validates the input, creates a job resource, enqueues the work, and returns 202 Accepted with the job's URL (in a Location header and in the body). The client polls GET /summaries/{id}. That returns the status and, when done, the result or a link to it. Alternatively, the server pushes completion by webhook, SSE or a message on a topic.

The result is stored, so polling never re-runs the model. Example 04_long_running_202.py asserts exactly one model call after three polls. Add an idempotency key on the POST, and a retried submission returns the same job instead of starting a second one.
0b4d570006:
An interactive chat needs a different answer: stream. Chapter 06 covers the Messages API's server-sent events, and chapter 14 the wire format. Streaming does not shorten total generation time. But the user sees the first words in about a second, and the connection is never idle, so intermediaries do not cut it.

The rule of thumb:

  • a human watching, and the answer arriving in under a minute: stream;
  • nobody watching, or longer work: 202 plus a job;
  • nobody watching, and the result needed tomorrow: the Batch API (chapter 07).
18aca9e80b:
JSON is the contract format everywhere in a Claude application: your API's bodies, the Messages API's request and response, tool definitions and tool inputs, structured outputs, logs and eval datasets.

You know how to validate JSON a client sends you. The new case is JSON that a model wrote, and it needs a different mindset. The model is not a malicious client, but it is not a typed program either. Ask the right way, and its output is very likely to have the right shape. However you ask, it is somewhat likely to be wrong in meaning.
eba6143a7a:
So validation happens in two layers, and they must not be confused.

Syntactic, or schema, validity: the text parses as JSON, required fields are present, types and enums match, strings match patterns.

Semantic validity: the values are true and consistent. The stated total equals the sum of the line items. The date is not in the future. The account id exists. The category agrees with the evidence.

Tool use with an input_schema, and structured outputs with strict schemas, make the first layer very reliable. Nothing makes the second layer automatic. Chapter 18 treats output handling in depth. This section covers the engineering: where the schema lives, how validation is wired, and how failures flow.
0cf5e5f26b:
Define the schema once, in code, and derive everything else from it.

In Python that is a Pydantic model. Invoice.model_json_schema() produces the JSON Schema you pass as a tool's input_schema. Invoice.model_validate(call.input) validates the tool input. And the same model types your API's response.

In Java the equivalent is a record with Jakarta Bean Validation annotations, a schema generator for the tool definition (for example victools jsonschema-generator), and Jackson for binding.

The point is a single source of truth. A schema written by hand in the prompt and another in the code will drift. The drift will show up as validation failures nobody can explain.
a789ad871f:
Three schema-design rules carry most of the weight, and each prevents a specific failure.

Make absent-able fields optional and nullable. A required po_number on invoices that often have none forces the model to put something there. And it will: a plausible invented number.

Give enums an escape value (other plus a detail field, or unclear). Without one, an ambiguous input is forced into the nearest wrong category, and you cannot tell it from a confident correct one.

Normalise in code, not in the prompt where you can. Ask for the value as written. Then, in your validator, convert dates to ISO 8601, money to integer cents or Decimal, and phone numbers to E.164. There the conversion is deterministic and tested.
d00be4656c: If you use a tool or structured outputs, you never parse prose. But you will meet code that asks for "JSON only" in a prompt and calls json.loads on the text. The exam expects you to know why that fails, and what the fix is. Example 05_defensive_json_parse.py runs both versions over five realistic outputs:
65c2ee555a:
Note what the defensive version does not do: it does not repair truncated JSON. It checks stop_reason first and raises when it is max_tokens. A "repaired" object is missing exactly the fields the model had not reached yet, and that silent loss is worse than an exception.

It also refuses ambiguous output with two objects, rather than guessing which one was meant. The real fix is upstream: move the contract into a tool schema, so the question never arises.
cd704ddc6e:
When validation fails, one retry with specific feedback often fixes it. But only if the information is actually in the source. Send the model its previous tool call, and a tool_result with is_error: true naming the failing fields and rules.

Example 07_validate_retry_feedback.py shows both outcomes. A phone number written as (201) 555-0147 is corrected to E.164 on the second attempt. A request that never contained a number fails three different ways. The right outcome there is a human review queue, not a fourth attempt.

Cap the attempts (two or three) and log each failure with the prompt version. Track the validation-failure rate per prompt version as a quality metric. A jump after a prompt change is a regression your evals should have caught.
ede2e3d2e1:
An LLM call spends almost all of its time waiting. The request goes out, the model generates for several seconds, the response comes back. During that wait the calling thread does nothing useful.

In a thread-per-request server, each in-flight call pins one worker thread for its whole duration. With 200 Tomcat threads and calls that take 10 seconds, the server tops out at 20 requests per second while its CPU idles. The 201st concurrent user waits for a thread, not for Claude.
a73347ec09:
Asynchronous I/O fixes this by letting one thread wait on many sockets.

In Python the model is asyncio. A single-threaded event loop runs coroutines. Each await on network I/O yields the thread to other coroutines until the data arrives. The SDK provides AsyncAnthropic, with the same surface as the synchronous client, and FastAPI runs async def handlers on the event loop.

The contract of that model is strict: nothing on the event loop may block. One blocking call stops every other coroutine on that loop for its duration.
34396a88af:
The most common concurrency defect in Python LLM services is a synchronous SDK call inside an async def handler. It is also a favourite distractor. It looks harmless, and it works in a demo with one user. Under load it serialises every request on the worker.

Example 08_blocking_event_loop.py runs five concurrent 0.3-second "model calls" three ways, while a heartbeat coroutine tries to tick every 10 ms:
6950d1d439:
The blocking version takes five times as long. For a second and a half nothing else on that loop ran: no health checks answered, no streamed tokens flushed to other users, no timeouts fired.

The two fixes are equivalent here. The preferred one is the async client, awaited. When a library has no async version, the bridge is asyncio.to_thread, which moves the blocking call off the loop (as does FastAPI's rule that plain def handlers run in a thread pool).

Note the second defect in the broken version below as well: a new client per request. That throws away the connection pool and TLS sessions every time. Create one client at startup and share it.
b8e799fe75:
Async makes concurrency cheap for you, which makes it easy to overwhelm them.

asyncio.gather(*(summarise(t) for t in tickets)) over 10,000 tickets starts 10,000 requests at once. The API's rate limiter answers with a wall of 429s. The SDK's retries add more load. And the job ends up taking longer than a modest, steady rate would have.

Bound in-flight calls with a semaphore set below what your rate limits allow. Example 09_semaphore_fanout.py runs 200 items against a fake upstream that accepts 8 concurrent requests:
84d057d0e0:
How do you choose the bound? Work from token budgets, not request counts, because the API limits input and output tokens per minute as well as requests.

Here is the arithmetic. Say your tier allows 400,000 input tokens per minute for the model, and a typical call sends 4,000 input tokens and takes 5 seconds. Then one in-flight slot uses about 48,000 input tokens per minute (4,000 tokens × 12 calls per minute). About 8 slots saturate the input limit. Set the semaphore to 6 or 7 to leave headroom for other traffic in the organisation.

Prompt caching changes the arithmetic, because cache reads do not count toward input-token rate limits on most models (chapter 05; check the docs for your model). Measure, then put the bound in configuration so operations can change it without a deploy.
d3ece03507: Concurrency raises a question synchronous code never asked. When one of several concurrent calls fails, what happens to the others? There are two legitimate answers. Choose the wrong one and it costs you either correctness or money.
099788a72b:
For independent items (summarise 500 tickets), one failure must not affect the rest. Use asyncio.gather(..., return_exceptions=True), which returns each item's result or exception in place. Give each call its own timeout.

For all-or-nothing fan-out, a failure in one makes the others useless. Think of three sub-queries whose results together form one answer, or parallel subagents feeding one synthesis. Every second the others keep running is tokens you will throw away. Use asyncio.TaskGroup (Python 3.11+), which cancels the siblings as soon as one task fails.

Cancellation propagates into the SDK call, which closes the HTTP connection. With streaming, that stops generation on your side. Whether you are billed for tokens generated before the disconnect is a detail to check in the docs.
5aeea6a9a1:
Finally, per-call timeouts do not bound a request that makes many calls. An agent step that makes ten sequential calls, with a 60-second timeout each, can take ten minutes.

Give the whole request a deadline (async with asyncio.timeout(...) around the loop), derived from what the caller will wait for. Pass the remaining budget down. Example 11_timeouts_cancellation.py shows all three:
ca7a5e6127:
One more timeout fact surprises people. The SDK's default request timeout is long, minutes rather than seconds (chapter 05 gives the default), because legitimate generations can be long.

For an interactive endpoint, set an explicit timeout that matches your user-facing budget. Set max_tokens so the generation cannot outgrow it. For long outputs the SDKs expect streaming. They may refuse a non-streaming request whose max_tokens implies a very long generation (check the docs for the threshold).
427edc86e7:
A semaphore bounds how many calls run at once. It does not bound how many items are waiting. If a Kafka consumer or an HTTP endpoint accepts work faster than the semaphore lets it through, the backlog grows in memory. Eventually the process dies, or latency becomes absurd.

Backpressure is the mechanism by which a slow consumer slows the producer down, instead of buffering without limit. In asyncio the simplest form is a bounded asyncio.Queue(maxsize=N). When it is full, await q.put(item) waits, so the producer runs at the consumers' pace.

At the HTTP edge, backpressure means rejecting early with 503 and Retry-After when the queue is full. Don't accept work you cannot finish in time.
d3fce694ee:
A fixed semaphore also assumes you know the limit. Often you don't. The rate limit is per organisation and shared with other services. A batch job from another team can start at any moment. And capacity differs by model.

The robust answer is the one TCP uses for congestion control: additive increase, multiplicative decrease (AIMD). On each success, raise the concurrency limit slowly. On each 429, halve it. The limit converges on what the shared quota currently allows, and follows it when it moves.

Example 10_backpressure_aimd.py runs 400 items through a bounded queue and 32 workers. The upstream's capacity drops from 12 to 5 a third of the way through:
b5f1e9ff57:
For a Spring team the decision is mostly between three models.

Virtual threads (Java 21) are the least disruptive. Keep the blocking SDK call and imperative code, and run each task on a virtual thread. The JVM parks it cheaply while the HTTP call waits. You still need a Semaphore to bound concurrency, because virtual threads remove the thread-pool bound that used to limit you by accident. Beware pinning: on Java 21, a virtual thread blocked inside a synchronized block pins its carrier thread (JDK 24 removed most of this; check your JDK).

CompletableFuture with the SDK's async client composes calls without blocking. It is a good fit when the code already uses futures.

Reactor/WebFlux gives backpressure natively: flatMap(fn, concurrency) bounds in-flight work, and demand propagates upstream. But it brings the reactive programming model with it.

The Anthropic Java SDK offers both synchronous and asynchronous clients. Check its docs for the exact async entry point.
844c9467e8:
In an LLM application, behaviour is defined by more than source code. It also comes from system prompts, few-shot examples, tool names, descriptions and schemas, the model ID, sampling and thinking settings, CLAUDE.md and .claude/settings.json, MCP configuration, and eval datasets and their thresholds. Any of them can change outputs. So all of them belong under the same version control and review as the code that uses them.

Chapter 10 owns the mechanics of configuration management: how to pin model versions, how to name and load prompt versions, what goes in settings.json versus settings.local.json, and how plugin dependencies are declared.

This section covers the workflow: where prompts sit in the repository, how changes to them flow through branches and pull requests, and what a reviewer needs to see.
992d60b119:
Keep each prompt in the same repository as the code that renders and calls it, ideally in the same module. Store it as a plain text or Markdown file (or a typed template), not as a string literal buried in a function. There are three reasons.

First, a prompt and its parsing code are a pair. A prompt change that renames an output field breaks the validator, so they must change in the same commit.

Second, the pull request diff of a prompt file is readable. The diff of a 60-line string literal with escaped newlines is not.

Third, the eval dataset and thresholds that judge the prompt sit beside it. The evidence for a change travels with the change.
089dec2ccc:
Storing prompts in a database or a prompt-management service is a legitimate choice when non-engineers edit them, or when you need runtime switching. It does not exempt them from review.

The service must give you immutable versions, an audit trail, a review step, and the ability to pin a version from code. The call site still logs which version produced each output. A prompt edited live in a console with no history is the LLM equivalent of patching a production JAR by hand.
7624677649:
Long-lived branches hurt more with prompts than with code, because prompt changes do not merge semantically. Git will happily merge two edits to different paragraphs of a system prompt. The result can contradict itself ("always offer a credit" from one branch, "never promise credits" from the other), with no conflict marker.

The working pattern is trunk-based. Use short-lived branches, with one logical prompt change per pull request, merged after tests and evals pass. Put the new behaviour behind a feature flag or a configuration switch, so deploying the code and releasing the behaviour are separate steps.

That is also how you run a canary (section 10). The flag routes 5% of traffic to triage@8 while 95% stays on triage@7.
8d8555ab4f:
When a model writes code in your repository (Claude Code, or an agent in CI), version control gains a second job. It becomes the safety net for the agent's actions.

Work on a branch or a separate git worktree. Commit in small steps, so you can bisect. Never let an agent push to the main branch directly. Claude Code's checkpoints help you rewind its edits within a session, but they are no substitute for commits (chapter 11 covers Claude Code operation).
7bcf742a73:
A pull-request template makes the evidence routine. For any change touching prompts/, tools.py, model configuration or eval thresholds, require the author to attach:

  • the rendered-request snapshot diff;
  • the eval report against the base branch, with per-category scores;
  • any new eval cases added for the behaviour being changed;
  • the rollout plan (flag name, canary percentage, rollback trigger).

CODEOWNERS can route prompt directories to the people accountable for the feature's behaviour, just as you route database migrations to the DBA team.
24eb6ad96e:
The life cycle does not change: requirements, design, build, test, release, operate, learn. Chapter 04 covers requirements and the life cycle at the product level.

What changes for engineering are two stages. The test stage changes, because a test suite of exact assertions cannot specify a model's behaviour. The operate stage changes, because quality can drift without any deploy. A provider-side model snapshot is fixed, but your input distribution is not, and an unpinned alias can move.
f8152f3717:
The answer is to add an evaluation suite as a first-class pipeline stage.

An eval is a dataset of representative inputs, each labelled with expected properties: the right category, the facts that must appear, the things that must not. It also has graders. Use code where the property is checkable (exact match on a category, schema validity, a regex for a forbidden promise). Use a model grader with a rubric where it is not. Add human review on samples.

Evals run on every change that can alter behaviour: prompt, tool description, model ID, retrieval configuration. They report per category, and the gate is per category. An aggregate can hide a collapse in a small but important slice.
2bd6ffa37c:
The division is clean once you state it.

Unit tests cover everything deterministic around the model: request rendering, tool dispatch, validation, idempotency, error mapping, retry classification, concurrency limits. They use fakes (section 11), run in seconds, never call the network, and must pass on every commit.

Evals cover the model's behaviour with your prompt. Does it classify correctly, extract the right fields, refuse what it should, avoid promising credits? Evals call the real model, cost money and take minutes. They report rates rather than pass/fail per case, and they gate merges of behaviour-changing changes.

Mixing the two gives you the worst of both. You get flaky unit tests that call the API and fail when it is slow, or "evals" that run against a fake and measure nothing.
4598a4669f:
Version 8 of the prompt improves three categories and the overall score. It also breaks number porting: the smallest category and, for a carrier, one with regulatory deadlines.

An aggregate gate ships it. A per-category gate blocks it and names the slice. This is the most-tested SDLC idea in the Anthropic exams (it appears in CCAR-F and CCAR-P sample questions too). Measure per category, and fix any category below its bar before launch.
bc9b942b88:
Three details in that workflow are deliberate.

The unit job has no API key. That guarantees the unit tests cannot accidentally call the network.

The eval job uses a separate key, in its own workspace with its own spend limit. A runaway eval cannot exhaust production quota.

And the eval compares against the base branch rather than a fixed number. The question for a pull request is "did this change make things worse", not "is the absolute score high".

For the eval run itself, a few hundred cases at realtime prices is normal for pull requests. A full regression over tens of thousands of cases is a good fit for the Batch API on a nightly schedule (chapter 07).
c728ff9639:
Release behaviour changes gradually. Start in shadow mode when you can: run the new prompt on live inputs, log its outputs, don't act on them, and compare. Then run a canary behind a flag, with automatic rollback on a quality or error-rate trigger. Then roll out fully.

In operation, log the prompt version, model ID, request-id, stop_reason, token usage, latency and validation outcome for every call. Chapter 12 shows how to use those traces to decide whether a failure is in the integration layer or in the model's output.

Sample production outputs for human review on a schedule. Turn every confirmed failure into a new eval case, so it cannot silently return.
436ca29766: The model is the one component you cannot unit test. So the design goal is to make everything else testable without it. That needs a seam: a point where the real client can be swapped for a test double. Meszaros' vocabulary helps you choose the right double, because they are not interchangeable.
d0736c0d42:
Every companion folder in this guide uses a recording fake. FakeClient mimics the response shape (content blocks, stop_reason, usage) and records every request in client.calls. So a test can assert both what came back and what was sent.

That second half is underrated. Many LLM bugs are request bugs: the system prompt missing after a refactor, untrusted text concatenated into the system prompt instead of delimited in the user turn, max_tokens too small for the schema, the tool list empty. A recording fake catches all of them for free.
b4536fffad:
Record/replay sits between fakes and live calls. You call the real API once, store the response in a "cassette" file committed to the repository, and replay it in CI.

The trap is the key. Some libraries key cassettes by URL alone, and every Messages API call has the same URL. They will replay the answer to the old prompt after you change it. Your tests stay green while testing nothing.

Key the cassette by a hash of the request fields that determine behaviour: model, system, messages, tools, tool choice. Then a prompt edit causes a loud miss and a deliberate re-record. Example 13_record_replay.py:
e0a0737ce2:
The rendered request (system prompt, tool definitions, message template filled with a fixed input) is deterministic code output. So it can be pinned with a golden file.

The test does not judge the prompt. It makes every change to the prompt show up as a readable diff in the pull request, next to the code change that caused it, where a reviewer cannot miss it. Example 14_prompt_snapshot.py produces this diff when a refactor silently dropped a rule:
f76039888c:
The risk of a fake is drift: it keeps passing while the real adapter's behaviour changes. The fix is a contract test, one test function run against every implementation of the interface.

In example 12_llm_port_interface.py, contract_test(impl) asserts that any TriagePort returns a Triage with urgency in range and a prompt version set. It runs against the Claude adapter (with a recorded or faked SDK underneath) and against FakeTriage. When someone changes the adapter to return a different shape, the contract fails before the service tests start lying.
640353b6fc:
Most LLM code starts life as a function that does everything. It reads the HTTP request, builds a prompt by string concatenation, calls the SDK, parses the text, writes to the database and returns.

It works. But it cannot be tested without the network, it cannot be reused, and it spreads SDK types through the codebase. When a second team wants triage, they copy the function. When the model ID changes, someone greps. This is the shape the exam's "refactoring" questions describe.
58792f60bf:
The target shape is hexagonal.

  • Business code depends on a port: a small interface in domain terms (triage(text) -> Triage), owned by the domain.
  • An adapter implements the port with Claude. It renders the request from a versioned prompt, calls the SDK, validates the output, and translates SDK exceptions into port-level ones (TriageUnavailable).
  • A fake implements the same port for tests.

Nothing outside the adapter imports the SDK. You have made the same move for payment gateways and HLR lookups. The domain says what it needs; the adapter knows how one vendor provides it.
8652d634d9:
Design the port in domain terms, not model terms. triage(text) -> Triage is good. complete(prompt) -> String is a wrapper around the SDK with a different name, and it leaves prompt-building and parsing scattered across every caller.

A generic "LLM client" interface still has its place, one layer down. The adapter may use a shared, instrumented client with retries, metrics and logging. But the business code should see capabilities, not completions.

The payoff goes beyond tests. Say you switch a capability to a cheaper model, to a rule engine for easy cases, or to the Batch API for a nightly variant. Each becomes a new adapter, not an edit to every caller.
5d63b12f0e:
The legacy function has no tests, so you cannot refactor it safely yet.

Feathers' answer is characterization tests. These pin what the code does today, oddities included. Run it against a recording fake, and assert the request it sends, the value it returns and the rows it writes.

Then refactor in small steps, running the characterization tests after each one. Only after the structure is clean do you fix the bugs the tests documented. Fix each in its own commit, so the behaviour change is visible in history and review.

Example 17_characterization_refactor.py does exactly this, and finds that the legacy function executes model output as SQL:
d629ff3262:
Look at the third and fourth lines. In the legacy code, a model output containing a quote rewrote every ticket's category, because the f-string SQL treated model text as code.

That is a prompt-injection path even without a malicious user. Any ticket text that persuades the model to echo a quote reaches the database. The refactored repository uses a parameterised query, so the same output is stored as an odd but harmless string.

Notice too that the refactor deliberately preserved the JSONDecodeError on prose output. Fixing that is a separate, visible step (move to a forced tool).
0db7f74bc1:
When Claude Code performs the refactor, the same discipline applies with more force, because it can change forty files in a minute.

  • Use plan mode to agree on the target shape and the sequence of steps before any edits.
  • Ask for one step per commit, with tests run between.
  • Keep the characterization tests out of the agent's write scope, or review any change to them with suspicion. An agent that edits the test to match its output has defeated the purpose.

Chapter 11 covers plan mode and permissions. Chapter 20 covers hooks that can block edits to protected paths.
ecf7ccc36d: Much of that table is mechanically checkable, and it should be checked by machine, so that human attention goes to what machines cannot judge. Example 16_review_lint.py is a 40-line AST linter that flags five of the defects in a typical first draft:
4ad97a3b6d:
A model reviewer is good at reading a whole diff patiently. It spots missing error handling, inconsistent naming, unhandled edge cases, and the kind of security smell that is visible in local code.

It is weak at three things: knowing your business rules unless told, judging whether a design fits the system, and being quiet. An unconstrained reviewer produces many low-value comments. Reviewers who see too many false positives stop reading any of them.

The practices that make it useful are the same ones CCAR-F tests (objectives 3.6 and 4.6), and they carry over directly.
fbb40e8af1: Use an independent instance. The session that wrote the code keeps its own reasoning and tends to confirm it. Review in a fresh context (a separate API call, a new Claude Code session, or a subagent). It should see the diff and the conventions, not the authoring conversation.
e9b5fca8ed: Tell it what is already known. Pass the linter's findings and previous review comments, so it reports only new issues. Example 16 sends them in a <known_findings> block.
08ac820ced: Ask for structured, line-anchored output. Use a forced tool or --json-schema with file, line, severity and issue. Then CI can post inline comments, and decide whether to fail the build on high severity.
6a394f016b: Split large diffs. Run per-file passes for local issues, plus one cross-file pass for integration issues (an interface changed in one file and not its callers). That beats one huge prompt.
64febee9a3:
The second half of the question is reviewing AI-authored code, which now makes up a large share of many diffs. Treat it as code from a capable new colleague who has read every public repository and none of your design documents. It compiles and reads well. That is exactly why plausible errors slip through.

The patterns to look for:

  • tests that assert what the code does rather than what it should do, or that mock away the unit under test;
  • happy-path correctness with missing timeout, empty-input and partial-failure handling;
  • calls to library functions or parameters that do not exist (types and CI catch most);
  • unrequested refactors and reformatting that bury the real change;
  • conventions silently ignored, because they were never written down.

The last one has a structural fix. Put conventions in CLAUDE.md and path-scoped rules files, so they are applied when the code is written, not discovered at review (chapter 10 and chapter 11).
15a8fffaa4: Insist on small diffs. A reviewer can genuinely review two hundred lines; nobody reviews four thousand. Ask the agent for one logical change per commit, with a message that says why. Reject pull requests that mix a refactor with a behaviour change. Small commits also make git bisect useful when an AI-written change turns out to have caused an incident three weeks later.
911a5b8421: Every row below is a pattern that appears in real LLM codebases and in exam distractors. The middle column is the mechanism. That is what lets you reject a distractor you have not seen before.
41796ef592:
The harm is a duplicated side effect, not a duplicated model call. The gateway retried the whole handler after provisioning had run.

A and D make timeouts rarer, but leave the next one just as harmful. B does nothing about the outer retry, and makes transient errors fail more. A business key makes any number of retries provision once. Timeout tuning can follow, as tuning.
41118bb8d2:
Low CPU, no 429s, latency proportional to concurrency, and failing health checks: that is the signature of a blocked event loop. Each blocking call serialises the worker.

A contradicts the headers. C hides the defect by multiplying processes and memory. D would make queuing worse. The handler also builds a client per request, a second defect the fix removes.
1e4cc1fb67:
Nobody is waiting on individual results, and the deadline is hours away. That is the Batch API's use case, at a lower price and outside the realtime rate limits (chapter 07). If the job had to stay realtime, the fix would be a semaphore sized from the token budget.

A and D add load to an already rate-limited path. C is still unbounded relative to the quota.
3017f86338:
The aggregate rose while one category fell (from 93% to 87% in example 15). Only a per-category gate exposes that.

A cannot help: a fake does not exercise the model's behaviour. C still lets a small category hide inside a large average. D reduces noise, but does not change what is measured.
cbff4c7749:
Without tests, nothing tells you whether the refactor preserved behaviour. And tests written after an AI rewrite tend to pin whatever the new code does. So: characterization tests first, then small steps toward a port and adapter, with the bug fixes visible as their own changes.

C wraps the SDK without separating concerns. D is a prompt-level mitigation for a code-level injection; the fix is a parameterised query.
14d1e3fdc7:
Done when: you can do all of this without notes:

  • explain why the side effect, not the model call, needs the idempotency key;
  • map any upstream failure to your own status code;
  • spot a blocked event loop from its symptoms;
  • size a semaphore from a token budget;
  • say which tests use fakes and which use the real model;
  • describe the review pipeline for a pull request that changes a prompt.
